title: Death as return
hook: death as a return, not an ending (2:156; 3:185)

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-'Asr, and your line: by time. Did you catch the light at two different hours? Time runs out for everyone, and today the book says where it runs to. Day six hundred eighty-six, the end of a week.

When a Muslim hears that someone has died, a neighbor's father, a celebrity, a friend's baby, the first words are very often the same. Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. People say it in hospital corridors, in group chats, under their breath at the news, before they've even taken it in. And if you listen to the words, they don't mention death at all. They talk about going back home.

Al-Baqarah, verse one hundred fifty-six, describes the patient as those who, when a misfortune strikes them, say, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Two halves. We belong to Allah. And to Him we return. Raji'un comes from r-j-', the root of going back to where you came from. Death, in this sentence, isn't a wall. It's a road home. Al 'Imran adds the plain fact underneath: "Every soul will taste of death." No exceptions, and the verse says it without fear: the full reward comes on the Day of Resurrection. Between death and that Day, the Qur'an speaks of a barzakh, a barrier, a waiting, in surah twenty-three. What it's like, the Qur'an doesn't describe in detail; the hadith say more, and scholars discuss them carefully. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows the words at work. Umm Salamah heard the Prophet ﷺ teach that whoever is struck by loss and says, to Allah we belong and to Him we return, and asks Allah to reward them and replace it with better, will be given better. When her husband Abu Salamah died, she said it, and thought, who could be better than Abu Salamah? Later the Prophet himself proposed to her. And graves aren't to be avoided. Another hadith in Muslim's collection says: I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them. A second report there gives a reason: they remind you of death. A cemetery, in this vocabulary, isn't the place where things end. It's a waiting room for a return.

The practice: visit a grave, or remember one. If you can visit a grave this week, plan when. For now, sit and bring to mind someone who has died. See their face, their hands, the sound of their voice. Don't push the grief away if it comes. Then, if you'd like, say the words softly: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. We belong to Allah, and to Him we return. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them. Stay with them a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Raji'un. Returning: in 2:156 the patient say we belong to Allah and to Him we are raji'un, going back to where we came from. Today's word.

Your line: a return. This week ran from no compulsion, read it in context, held in trust, parents come next and don't spoil it, to by time. Today, tell someone one good memory of a person who has died. Day six hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" on hearing of a death or any loss; they bury the dead quickly, pray the funeral prayer together, and visit graves, greeting the dead with peace.

trapdoor: what you thought: inna lillahi is the Muslim way of saying rest in peace.
what it means: we belong to Allah and to Him we return: death as a road home, said at any loss.
what a scholar hears: raji'un, from r-j-', return to where you began; 23:100 names the barzakh between death and the Day.
